plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 13: Structure Determination: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a perspective pictorial schematic of a basic NMR spectrometer, laying out sample, magnet, and signal path in one view. At the center a slender glass tube holding an orange column of sample solution stands upright, tagged "Sample in tube" by a leader line; a green helical coil wraps the tube's midsection between two blue collars. Two cylindrical magnet pole pieces face the coil from either side, the left one lettered S and the right one lettered N. At lower left a beige benchtop unit with knobs, small colored buttons, and a green digital readout showing 9.56 is labeled "Radiofrequency generator", and green leads run from it up to the coil. Blue cables leave the coil to the right and enter a dark gray box with two dials and a green and a red pushbutton, labeled "Detector and amplifier", from which further blue cables climb to a flat-panel monitor at the upper right. The monitor shows a pale blue field crossed by a red baseline carrying several sharp vertical peaks of unequal height. The left-to-right arrangement traces energy from generator to sample to detector to display, letting the reader follow one absorption event to a plotted line. The drawing introduces the instrument in which a strong field aligns 1H and 13C nuclei and swept field strength brings each into resonance separately.

beige radiofrequency generator box (bottom left, green display '9.56', colored buttons)
dark gray detector and amplifier box (bottom right, dials, red and green buttons)
black flat-panel monitor (top right, light blue screen with red spectrum trace)
green wires connecting RF generator to the coil
blue wires connecting the coil to the detector
blue wires connecting the detector to the monitor

interactions.label: Magnetic Field
interactions.teaches: Sweeping the magnetic field brings different sets of nuclei into resonance at a constant RF frequency, producing distinct peaks on the spectrum.
Selecting a component highlights its role in the signal path, tracing energy from RF generation to sample excitation, detection, and final display.

demo_steps.title: Baseline Field
demo_steps.narration: The sample sits in a low magnetic field. The RF generator is active, but the field is not yet strong enough to bring any nuclei into resonance.

demo_steps.title: First Resonance
demo_steps.narration: At a specific field strength, the first set of nuclei (e.g., protons in one chemical environment) come into resonance, absorbing and re-emitting RF energy to form a peak.

demo_steps.title: Second Resonance
demo_steps.narration: At a higher field strength, a different set of nuclei achieve resonance, producing a second distinct peak on the monitor.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Center sample tube at (0, 0, 0), height 6, diameter 0.4. Magnet poles: cylinders diameter 3, height 1.5, gap ±1.2 from center. S magnet at (-2, 0, 0), N magnet at (2, 0, 0), labels 'S' and 'N' on their front/side faces. RF Generator: Box 2.5 x 1.5 x 1.5 at (-4.5, -2.5, 1), beige #EEDDCC. Detector: Box 1.5 x 2.5 x 1.5 at (3, -2.5, 1), dark gray #333333. Monitor: Box 3 x 2 x 0.2 at (5, 2, -1) with light blue screen #AADDFF. Coil: Green #2CA02C helix around the tube, radius 0.25, height 2. Nuclei: ~15 small spheres (radius 0.05) scattered inside the orange sample liquid.
interactionPlan.notes: For the 'componentFocus' click interaction, implement a raycaster: clicking the RF generator highlights it and the green wires; clicking the coil highlights it and the sample; clicking the detector highlights it and the lower blue wires; clicking the monitor highlights it and the upper blue wires. For the 'magneticFieldStrength' slider, simulate the resonance sweep: when the slider is near 3.5 (±0.3), scale up 5 nuclei spheres and color them bright yellow, and draw the left red peak on the monitor screen. When near 7.5 (±0.3), flash the other 10 nuclei and draw the taller right red peak. When outside these narrow windows, keep nuclei faint and peaks hidden to emphasize that resonance is a discrete matching condition.

authoredContext:
The operation of a basic NMR spectrometer is illustrated in the figure. An organic sample is dissolved in a suitable solvent (usually deuteriochloroform, CDCl3, which has no hydrogens) and placed in a thin glass tube between the poles of a magnet. The strong magnetic field causes the 1H and 13C nuclei in the molecule to align in one of the two possible orientations, and the sample is irradiated with rf energy. If the frequency of the rf irradiation is held constant and the strength of the applied magnetic field is varied, each nucleus comes into resonance at a slightly different field strength. A sensitive detector monitors the absorption of rf energy, and its electronic signal is then amplified and displayed as a peak.

Schematic operation of a basic NMR spectrometer. A thin glass tube containing the sample solution is placed between the poles of a strong magnet and irradiated with rf energy.

Schematic diagram of spectrometer shows sample in tube placed between south and north poles. Tube connects to radiofrequency generator (left) and detector and amplifier (right), which further connects to monitor.

NMR spectroscopy differs from IR spectroscopy (another section–another section) in that the timescales of the two techniques are quite different. The absorption of infrared energy by a molecule giving rise to a change in vibrational amplitude is an essentially instantaneous process (about 10–13 s), but the NMR process is much slower (about 10–3 s). This difference in timescales between IR and NMR spectroscopy is analogous to the difference between cameras operating at very fast and very slow shutter speeds. The fast camera (IR) takes an instantaneous picture and freezes the action. If two rapidly interconverting species are present, IR spectroscopy records the spectrum of both. The slow camera (NMR), however, takes a blurred, time-averaged picture. If two species interconverting faster than 103 times per second are present in a sample, NMR records only a single, averaged spectrum, rather than separate spectra of the two discrete species.

Blue cables leave the coil to the right and enter a dark gray box with two dials and a green and a red pushbutton, labeled "Detector and amplifier", from which further blue cables climb to a flat-panel monitor at the upper right. The monitor shows a pale blue field crossed by a red baseline carrying several sharp vertical peaks of unequal height. The left-to-right arrangement traces energy from generator to sample to detector to display, letting the reader follow one absorption event to a plotted line. The drawing introduces the instrument in which a strong field aligns 1H and 13C nuclei and swept field strength brings each into resonance separately.
